title: Deep Learning Systems and Practice
description: Training strategies, efficient inference, and neural-model evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is a common benefit of mixed-precision training?
options: Lower memory use and faster supported arithmetic
Guarantee identical results on every device
questions.explanation: Lower-precision operations can improve throughput and memory use, often while retaining higher-precision accumulations.

questions.prompt: Numerically stable implementations can matter when evaluating exponentials and logarithms.
questions.explanation: Extreme values can overflow or underflow; stable forms such as log-sum-exp reduce these risks.

questions.prompt: What does gradient accumulation enable when memory is limited?
options: Approximate a larger effective batch across several smaller batches
Fit a larger model without any compute
questions.explanation: Accumulating gradients before an optimizer step combines multiple minibatches into a larger effective batch.

questions.prompt: In data-parallel training, what do multiple workers typically process?
options: Different minibatches using replicas of the model
One weight each with no synchronization
questions.explanation: Workers compute gradients on separate data shards and synchronize updates or gradients.

questions.prompt: Which can limit distributed training speedup?
options: Using more workers always reduces runtime
questions.explanation: Communication and imbalance can dominate; additional workers do not guarantee faster training.

questions.prompt: Why optimize a deep-learning input pipeline?
options: To keep accelerators supplied with data
To change the model’s labels at runtime
questions.explanation: A slow loader can leave expensive accelerators idle, limiting end-to-end throughput.

questions.prompt: What is throughput in inference serving?
options: Number of requests or examples processed per unit time
Time to answer one request only
questions.explanation: Throughput measures processing rate; it is distinct from individual request latency.

questions.prompt: Dynamic batching can increase throughput but may add waiting time for individual requests.
questions.explanation: Combining requests can use hardware efficiently, while waiting to form batches can increase latency.

questions.prompt: What does model quantization generally do?
options: Represent weights or activations with lower-precision values
Increase the number of training labels
questions.explanation: Quantization reduces numerical precision to save storage or accelerate execution, with possible quality trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What is neural-network pruning?
options: Removing or zeroing selected parameters or structures
Converting all layers to recurrent ones
questions.explanation: Pruning removes less useful weights or structures; practical speedups depend on hardware and sparse-kernel support.

questions.prompt: In knowledge distillation, what is commonly transferred from teacher to student?
options: A training signal from a larger model
The teacher’s source-code license as learned data
questions.explanation: Distillation uses teacher outputs and sometimes hidden features to train a smaller student.

questions.prompt: Why pin a model and preprocessing version in a serving release?
options: Ensure predictions use compatible artifacts and transformations
questions.explanation: Version alignment prevents an artifact from receiving inputs transformed under incompatible logic.

questions.prompt: What does post-hoc calibration aim to improve?
options: Agreement between predicted confidence and empirical correctness
questions.explanation: Calibration adjusts confidence estimates to better reflect observed frequencies without necessarily changing ranking.

questions.prompt: A high score on one benchmark proves a model will perform reliably in every deployment setting.
questions.explanation: Benchmarks cover limited data and tasks; deployment conditions and failure modes may differ.

questions.prompt: What is an out-of-distribution input?
options: An input unlike the data conditions represented during training
An example with a valid label
A model checkpoint saved outside the cloud
questions.explanation: Distributionally novel inputs can cause uncertain or unreliable predictions and may need separate handling.

questions.prompt: Which tests can probe neural-model robustness?
options: Test adversarial or worst-case examples where relevant
questions.explanation: Robustness testing explores perturbations and shifts; training loss alone says little about behavior under such changes.

questions.prompt: What does saliency analysis commonly attempt to show?
options: Which input regions or features influence a prediction under a chosen method
A proof that the model is fair
The exact training data for every weight
questions.explanation: Saliency methods estimate input sensitivity or attribution and should be interpreted with method-specific limitations.

questions.prompt: Setting a random seed guarantees bit-for-bit identical results across all hardware and software versions.
questions.explanation: Seeds improve repeatability, but kernels, hardware, parallelism, and library versions can still introduce variation.

questions.prompt: What should guide autoscaling for a neural inference service?
options: Observed demand, latency objectives, and resource utilization
The number of model layers alone
A fixed maximum batch size only
questions.explanation: Scaling policies should reflect request patterns and service-level targets as well as compute constraints.

questions.prompt: Which telemetry is useful for a model-serving service?
options: Input and prediction distributions with privacy safeguards
questions.explanation: Operational and model-behavior metrics support diagnosis; telemetry should avoid unnecessary sensitive-data retention.
